title: The Things Iroh Cannot Carry
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 32 of 40
content:
The bed shook once beneath me.

Not from an earthquake. Iroh had sat upright so quickly that the mattress shifted against the wall. The room above the Jasmine Dragon was dark, and his hand had closed around the blanket until the cloth twisted like a rope.

"Iroh?"

He did not answer.

Rain tapped the roof tiles. Down below, a cart rolled past the shuttered shop, its wheels catching on the same loose paving stone I had been meaning to report. An ordinary night in Ba Sing Se. I said the city aloud, slowly.

"We're upstairs. It's raining. There's a cart outside."

His breathing changed.

He looked toward the door.

"Jasper?"

"Here."

"Forgive me. I must have disturbed you."

"You did wake me." I pulled the blanket back over my knees. "That's different from asking for forgiveness."

I could see his expression only when the street lantern caught the side of his face. He looked tired in a way that didn't belong to one bad dream.

"Would you like a light?" I asked.

"A small one."

I lit the lamp near the window. I didn't touch him, though I wanted to. His fingers were still curled against the blanket.

"Do you want me close?"

"Yes. Not suddenly."

I moved beside him and rested my hand open between us. After a moment he took it.

The quiet stretched. He wasn't going to tell me what he'd dreamed, and I didn't want to turn the silence into an interrogation.

Then he said, "In the dream, I knew where the men were going. I kept sending them anyway."

I thought of the siege he rarely described and the grief that had followed him long after the fighting stopped.

"You don't have to finish that sentence."

"I know. I wish knowing it made the memory less loud."

He swallowed.

"I am very good at telling other people to rest. I am considerably less talented at obeying myself."

"That sounds familiar."

He looked at me.

"You?"

"I can organize a whole square after a flood, then forget to eat until someone points at a bowl."

"An appalling habit."

"Yours or mine?"

"Both."

He laughed once, without much joy.

I asked whether he wanted tea. He said no; he didn't want to go downstairs and start treating the night like another shift. We stayed where we were until his hand relaxed.

"Would it help to speak to someone about the nightmares?" I asked eventually.

He looked toward the lamp.

"Someone outside this room?"

"Someone you choose. It doesn't have to be me."

His face tightened.

"Are you tired of listening?"

I was hurt by the question, then felt ashamed of being hurt.

"No. I'm saying I can love you and still not know how to help with every part of what you carry. I don't want my being here to become the only thing between you and a night like this."

He considered that. There was no comfortable way to tell someone I loved that I wasn't a cure, but I wanted him to believe I wasn't leaving because I said it.

"I know a healer who works with veterans," he said finally. "She has written to me before."

"Would you like to write back?"

"Perhaps in the morning."

"Then in the morning."

He set the lamp lower. I rested against him only after he moved his arm to make room. We did not go back to sleep quickly.

At dawn, Mina knocked on the downstairs door. Someone had arrived early with a delivery and needed the dry-goods store opened.

Iroh started to rise.

"I can get it," I said. "You're allowed to stay upstairs."

"Are you certain?"

"I can open a door and sign a receipt. I've had extensive training."

He smiled.

Mina and I checked the jars, rejected one cracked lid, and recorded the shortage. She didn't ask about our night. I didn't offer it.

When I returned with breakfast, Iroh had placed a clean sheet of paper beside his cup.

"I have written a letter," he said.

"To the healer?"

"Yes."

He hesitated.

"I have not told her the dream. Only that I would like an appointment and that I prefer to speak privately."

"That sounds like enough to begin."

He looked relieved.

We took the letter to the post, then walked slowly along the sheltered market street. Rain had washed the stones dark. Iroh offered his arm, and I took it.

"I hope you do not think my weakness changes how I feel about you," he said.

"I don't think fear makes you weak."

"You have said that before."

"And you've listened before. We're both allowed to need another reminder."

At the corner, the baker was opening her shutters. She waved. Iroh waved back, a little shyly.

We had told each other about my ethical non-monogamy and preference for polyamory long before that morning. He knew I would cross to Lanternweald again, and that I loved other people. None of that changed how seriously I took what he'd trusted me with. I didn't promise to be the only person he could ask for help. I promised to remain truthful about when I could be here.

Back in the courtyard, he set out two cups. The first tea was too weak.

"Terrible," I said.

"An offense against civilization."

"Shall we try again?"

"Yes."

We made a second pot.

That evening he asked me to sit beside him while he read the healer's reply. I did. It offered a private appointment the following week. He wrote the date in his own calendar instead of asking me to manage it for him.

Later he kissed me softly, his fingers still warm from the cup. I kissed him back, and we closed the bedroom door on a night that belonged to us, not the war.

The nightmares had not vanished. But there was another name in the notebook, another kind of help, and a morning waiting after the dark.
